review_note: Keep the runbook structure, practical scripts, quiet teaching directions and support slide. Align the limits of the course’s model with the lecture; cut repeated declarations of significance and classroom predictions.

edits.before: Week 7: overload, shutdown, recovery. The last lecture before the break, on purpose.
edits.after: Week 7: overload, shutdown, recovery. A runbook before the break.
edits.reason: State the useful timing without announcing intentionality.

edits.before: - The break is when they'll have room to use what's here. Say that up front.
edits.after: - Thursday's lab is time to write the runbook and plan the break.
edits.reason: Point to the scheduled work without assuming the break gives every student free capacity.

edits.before: ## Why the framing earns its place here
edits.after: ## A runbook
edits.reason: Introduce the tool rather than asking the slide to prove the course’s metaphor has earned its place.

edits.before: - This is the week where the protocol framing is most useful rather than most clever. Don't oversell it; just use it.
edits.after: - Use the example of a saved absence message: one decision made before the difficult day.
edits.reason: Replace self-assessment of the framing with a concrete example.

edits.before: Week 6 gave you a ledger and a unit. Recovery hours, and the finding that **time spent** is the damaging axis.
edits.after: Week 6 gave you a ledger. **Recovery hours** are its planning unit; the research finding concerns **time spent camouflaging**.
edits.reason: Keep the recap consistent with week 6’s distinction between recovery time and exposure time.

edits.before: - And say why this lecture sits immediately before the break. It is not an accident of timetabling.
edits.after: - Ask them to bring their week 6 ledger to Thursday's runbook workshop.
edits.reason: Replace another announcement of deliberate scheduling with the preparation students can use.

edits.before: - Overload and shutdown recover in hours or a day. Burnout doesn't, and the difference decides what you do.
edits.after: - These are planning time scales, not recovery deadlines. The table distinguishes immediate load from load that has accumulated for weeks.
edits.reason: Align the note with the lecture’s limited model rather than giving an unsupported recovery promise.

edits.before: <MarginNote label="Errata, early">The map has four territories. This course drew three.</MarginNote>
edits.after: <MarginNote label="Errata, early">Two named states are missing from this map.</MarginNote>
edits.reason: BIMS and the course’s three rows are overlapping lists, not three entries from one four-entry list.

edits.before: - The good news: shutdown is not the course's coinage. The bad news is the other two.
edits.after: - Leave room in the runbook for states beyond the course's three rows.
edits.reason: Turn commentary about the course’s omissions into a useful instruction.

edits.before: - What it does establish: a runbook that addresses mood alone would miss most of what is happening.
edits.after: - Use the emotional, cognitive and physical components as prompts; do not present the three course rows as exhaustive.
edits.reason: Keep the practical application without claiming a measured proportion of experience would be missed.

edits.before: - That sequence is the week's quiet point: the people living it had the description first, and the literature caught up.
edits.after: - Keep the sequence clear: community descriptions preceded these research definitions.
edits.reason: Keep the historical point without telling the lecturer which revelation the week is engineered to deliver.

edits.before: - Community-based participatory approach. The definition came from the people it describes, which is the point.
edits.after: - Name the community-based participatory approach when introducing the definition.
edits.reason: Retain the method without appending another announcement of significance.

edits.before: - Their authors note the danger of teaching autistic people to mask. This course takes that seriously.
edits.after: - Their authors note the danger of teaching autistic people to mask.
edits.reason: The course’s claim to take the warning seriously adds no evidence or instruction.

edits.before: - So the load is real, it differs between groups in the same room, and it can be compared. That makes it a parameter, not a mood.
edits.after: - This is a comparison of reported discomfort in Swedish health care settings; do not imply that the questionnaire observed everyone in the same room.
edits.reason: Preserve the study’s setting and method rather than presenting it as a controlled room comparison.

edits.before:
- Most people find their earliest sign is invisible to everyone but them.
- That is exactly why it goes in a runbook instead of being left to be spotted. Land the debrief there.
edits.after: - If a sign would be hard for others to notice, ask what the student could tell them when it appears. Do not assume the room will share one answer.
edits.reason: Let the activity discover visibility rather than prescribing a result.

edits.before: - It is a planning checklist, and the whole room needs the break for something. One slide each.
edits.after: - Use the four experiences as a planning checklist. One slide each.
edits.reason: Keep the teaching instruction without assuming each student’s circumstances.

edits.before: - The hardest of the four for most students, and the one a phone defeats.
edits.after: - Ask which phone notifications bring work back into the break, and whether any could be turned off.
edits.reason: Replace unsupported rankings with an actionable question about detachment.

edits.before: - This is the one a family Christmas removes, and it is worth naming so nobody thinks they failed at resting.
edits.after: - A family visit can fill a calendar with obligations even without coursework. Use it as an example of limited control over time.
edits.reason: Keep the recognisable example without asserting that every family Christmas removes control.

edits.before:
A resolution is a decision you make **while** you are struggling. That is the worst possible time to make one.

A runbook is a decision made **in advance**, by the version of you with the most capacity, for the version with the least.
edits.after:
Trying to decide what to drop **while** you are struggling adds another decision to the load.

A runbook records those decisions **in advance**, when you have more capacity.
edits.reason: Replace a false definition of resolutions and a superlative with the actual benefit of preparing a runbook.

edits.before: - This distinction is the whole reason the week uses an engineering artefact rather than a wellbeing one.
edits.after: - Point forward to the six sections: each removes a decision from the difficult day.
edits.reason: Explain how the tool works instead of defending the genre of the lesson.

edits.before: ## Six sections, and the one that matters
edits.after: ## Six sections
edits.reason: Avoid ranking five required sections as though only the highlighted one matters.

edits.before: ## The section people skip
edits.after: ## What gets dropped
edits.reason: Remove the unsupported frequency claim from the slide heading.

edits.before: **What gets dropped.** And it's the one the burnout research supports most directly.
edits.after: Fill in **what gets dropped** before adding recovery activities.
edits.reason: Match the lecture’s practical instruction without over-ranking the evidence.

edits.before: - That is the fix recommended by the people who have it, and it is the single most important sentence in the week.
edits.after: - Link this instruction to participants' reports of time off and reduced expectations.
edits.reason: Keep the source connection and cut the repeated declaration of what matters most.

edits.before: - The delete-one-sentence step is the exercise. Everyone writes too much the first time.
edits.after: - The deletion tests which information the recipient needs. Ask what changed when that sentence came out.
edits.reason: Preserve the exercise without pretending every first draft is too long.

edits.before: - **overload · shutdown · burnout** --- three of the four named phenomena
edits.after: - **overload · shutdown · burnout** --- the course's three time scales
edits.reason: Overload is not one of the four BIMS terms; keep the two models distinct in the recap.
